Under moment conditions, summable physical dependence coefficients and a bracketing entropy condition controlling the infinite-dimensional tails, the centered partial sum process converges weakly in $D([0,1],B)$ to a centered Gaussian process, whose covariance is the integrated local long-run covariance, an element of the projective tensor product. We also obtain a stochastic integral representation with respect to a cylindrical Brownian motion. As the limit depends on the unknown long-run covariance, we prove consistency of a block multiplier bootstrap for the partial sum process. This yields CUSUM tests for a constant mean of the full process, based on arbitrary continuous seminorms and valid under a time-varying long-run covariance. For linear projections, we derive a self-normalized test with a pivotal limit. In simulations, the supremum norm test detects localized changes that its $L^2$ counterpart largely misses, and applications to EEG and temperature data illustrate the methodology. Examples in $C([0,1])$ and $W^{1,p}_0([0,1])$ show how the entropy condition can be verified.
item.dc:creator: Florian Heinrichs, Luis-Alberto Rodr\'iguez

item.title: Anchored multiple testing: a transparent use of e-closure to improve FDR procedures
item.description: arXiv:2610.11279v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The recent e-closure method can recover every procedure that controls FDR (and other expectation losses). But the recovered e-collection is ``self-referential'' and gives no insight on how to improve the procedure (if improvable), and some recent improvements have been somewhat opaque. We introduce an elementary new technique called anchoring that exploits looseness in existing FDR proofs to enlarge a baseline multiple-testing procedure's self-referential local e-value. The resulting e-closure thus transparently retains every baseline discovery (and usually adding more) and controlling the false discovery rate under the same conditions as the baseline. To show that this principle is broadly applicable, we use it to improve a large suite of multiple testing procedures: (i) Anchored-BH dominates the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure under PRDS while being incomparable to Goeman's recent closed-BH, (ii) Anchored-BY dominates the Benjamini-Yekutieli (BY) procedure under arbitrary dependence while being incomparable to closed-BY, (iii) For two-sided Gaussian p-values (under appropriate covariance conditions), Anchored-2BH dominates running BH twice at half the level on two one-sided p-values, (iv) Anchored-dBH dominates dependence-adjusted BH, (v) Anchored e-BH dominates e-BH and is incomparable to closed e-BH, (vi) Anchored SeqStep+ improves the original (including selective and adpative variants) while preserving ordered rejection structures. All of these are accomplished in sorting or quadratic time. The appendix shows how to dominate Shifted-BH (for two-sided arbitrarily correlated Gaussians) and NDBH (for negatively dependent p-values), IndBH (for graph-dependent p-values), conformal multiple testing and the support line procedure for boundary FDR control.
item.dc:creator: Aaditya Ramdas

item.title: Optimal Experimental Design for the Polynomial Maximization Method: a Higher-Order Reserve Beyond Second-Order Design Theory
item.description: arXiv:2610.33921v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Optimal designs for regression with asymmetric errors build on the second-order least squares estimator (SLSE) of Wang and Leblanc (2008), whose gain over ordinary least squares (OLS) comes from the error skewness. With i.i.d. errors the optimally weighted SLSE solves the same estimating equation as the degree-two Polynomial Maximization Method (PMM), a family whose degree-$S$ location estimator has asymptotic variance $g_S\le1$ times that of the sample mean. We derive optimal designs for this family when the errors are independent with constant variance but have standardised cumulants of order three and higher that vary with the regressor (cumulant heteroscedasticity). For a known reduction field $g_S(x)$, the $g_S$-weighted information matrix $M_{g_S}$ obeys the Kiefer-Wolfowitz equivalence theorem. A constant field leaves the OLS-optimal design unchanged; a non-constant field can change it but need not. For symmetric errors with varying kurtosis, the PMM$_2$ and conditional-SLSE designs cannot depart from the OLS-optimal one, whereas a degree-three design can. A stratify-and-pool PMM$_S$ estimator attains $N\mathrm{Cov}(\hat\theta)\to\sigma^2M_{g_S}^{-1}$ at every degree as all strata grow; its per-stratum reduction is below one only for symmetric errors with the symmetry imposed. For a quadratic model on $[0,1]$ with symmetric Beta errors of unit variance and dose-varying shape, the third-order design for the known field has $A$-efficiency $1.047$ relative to the OLS-optimal design, and $1.001$ under the $D$-criterion. A two-stage procedure that estimates the field from a one-third pilot builds designs of $A$-efficiency $1.014$-$1.020$ at $N=600$-$2400$; its realised mean-squared-error ratio against the OLS-optimal design ranges from $0.89$ (a loss) to $1.08$.
item.dc:creator: Serhii Zabolotnii

item.title: The German Tank Problem & Navigating by Scent
item.description: arXiv:2610.34583v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A robot searching for the source of an odor must eventually answer a notably hard question: have I arrived? Near the source, concentration gradients homogenize, turbulence corrupts the signal, and a small robot often lacks the positional accuracy to map the plume. Here, we describe a lightweight remedy inspired by a World War II statistics conundrum: the German tank problem. To approximate German armament production, Allied analysts developed an estimator based on serial numbers from captured tanks. Analogously, we use the same procedure over sampled chemical sensor readings from a robot to create estimates for the peak concentration of an odor plume, and therefore the odor's source. Treating each sensor reading as an observation, our unbiased estimator needs only a running maximum and a sample counter. A confidence bound turns both numbers into a principled rule that the robot or UAV can use to determine whether it should keep searching for the odor source. We derive the estimator and its bound, demonstrate its sample efficiency, and examine its robustness even when its assumptions fail. Finally, we summarize the estimator's role as the termination criterion for olfactory navigation.
item.dc:creator: Kordel Kade France
